 SF Gate Logo TOP STORY Plans to turn Bay Area mall from 'death spiral' into housing moves forward News | Politics There's a 'poison pill' that could doom the California billionaire tax
 Prop. 40 could fail even if it gets a majority of yes votes this year
 U.S. Director of the National Institutes of Health Jayanta Bhattacharya, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, entrepreneur Sergey Brin, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and AMD CEO Lisa Su attend the “Golden Age of American Innovation Summit” at the Institute of Peace in Washington, DC, on Oct. 8, 2026.
 Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images By Lester Black , News editor Oct 26, 2026 California’s  billionaire tax proposal has become one of the midterm elections’ most controversial measures, with the entire country watching to see if California’s voters will approve an unprecedented tax on billionaires’ net worth. 
 But before voters can actually say yes or no to the tax, they’ll have to figure out how to do it. 
 Approving Proposition 40, the tax on billionaires, is surprisingly complicated because there are two other competing ballot measures that contain “poison pill” language designed to cancel out Proposition 40. These other measures (Proposition 41 and Proposition 42) do not specifically say they are designed to kill the tax, and public polling shows that at least some voters who want to support the billionaire tax could be unknowingly planning to vote against it. 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 A group of billionaires has bankrolled the poison pill measures, and their opponents are calling it a way of tricking voters into accidentally voting against the new tax on the ultrawealthy.
 Here’s how the three competing measures directly stack up:
 Proposition 40 , commonly called the billionaire tax, would create a one-time, 5% tax on Californians who have over a billion dollars in net worth as of Jan. 1, 2026. The funds would primarily be used for healthcare.
 Proposition 41 would require audits of special statewide taxes and prohibit certain types of new taxes.
 Proposition 42 would block any new taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and would block new state taxes that apply retroactively to taxpayer conduct. 
 Neither Proposition 41 nor Proposition 42 specifically says it in its ballot language, but both contain language that is designed to nullify Proposition 40. That means even if voters approve Proposition 40, it could not become law if Proposition 41 or Proposition 42 receives more votes. Although if that happens, either side will likely file a lawsuit and bring the battle to the courts, which doesn’t make things any less confusing. 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 People attend a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in La Palma, Calif.
 Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW, the union backing the billionaire tax, called the tactics from the billionaires trying to block the wealth tax “deceptive” because they combined tax reforms that sound like common-sense measures.
 “This is not about trying to fix our tax system in any way. It’s about protecting billionaires’ interest and making sure billionaires are not taxed,” Jimenez said.
 Brian Marvel, the president of the Peace Officer Resource Association of California and a Proposition 42 supporter, said in an emailed statement that the measure is aimed at making sure retirement savings are always protected from taxation.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 “Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve,” Marvel said.
 An unprecedented tax on billionaires
 If passed, Proposition 40 would be the first modern tax on a person’s net worth — as opposed to a tax on income or a single asset’s worth, like real estate — and would bring in billions of dollars in revenue for the state. The historic nature of the initiative is making it a bellwether initiative for the entire country as inequality  soars to its highest levels since World War II.
 Some of California’s billionaires, like venture capitalist and Democratic politician Tom Steyer or Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, have said they have no problem paying a 5% tax given it’s a fraction of their colossal net worths. But other billionaires have taken the threat personally. Michael Moritz, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist, recently told the New York Times that billionaires “have become piñatas for politicians.”
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 A coalition including billionaires like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has bankrolled the opposition to Proposition 40, both by campaigning against the proposition but by also paying for Proposition 41 and Proposition 42. The ultrawealthy donors are on track to break fundraising records, with Brin alone donating $102 million to fight the progressive tax.
 Jimenez said she expects the total fight to swell to over $400 million, with billionaires funding a large part of it, which she said was a shocking amount of money to fight a tax to help low-income Californians.
 “I honestly think it’s shameful, it really speaks to what they think about everyday Californians and those who rely on the Medicaid system,” Jimenez said.
 Yes on 40 signs sit on seats at the “Ballots Over Billionaires” rally on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles.
 Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images Proponents say the tax is a necessary way to fill gaps in healthcare spending after Republicans in Congress gutted Medicaid, that a 5% tax is a small price for the world’s wealthiest people, and that there’s no risk of billionaires fleeing the state, as their numbers have actually increased since the proposal was announced. 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Critics say the billionaire tax is poor policy because it would raise funds only one time and could hurt the state in the long term by pushing billionaires and their tax payments out of state. Opponents have also claimed that Proposition 40 could eventually be expanded beyond billionaires to create new taxes for lower-income people. 
 The fear of the tax expanding to apply beyond the ultrarich is part of what the billionaires are tapping into with Proposition 42, which would make it illegal for financial assets like retirement accounts to face new state taxes. Newsom echoed this critique of Proposition 40 in his endorsement of Proposition 42, saying it was necessary to protect people’s “life savings.”
 Chris Micheli, an attorney, lobbyist and professor at the McGeorge School of Law in Sacramento, said neither side’s argument is totally correct. There’s no legal evidence that Proposition 40 could be expanded to non-billionaires, but if the ultrawealthy do start fleeing the state, it would be a problem for tax collections.
 “The state of California … is so dependent on the wealthiest Californians that if we lose some of those taxpayers, it seriously erodes our tax base, so that means our burden falls all over the rest of us,” Micheli said.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 ‘Poison pill’
 Political groups have long used California’s ballot initiative system to wage battles against each other with competing propositions, like in 2022, when two competing sports betting measures were on the ballot, or in 2016, when voters had to decide between two competing death penalty regulations. But Propositions 41 and 42 are unique in that they include language that directly attacks another measure rather than offering a competing proposal, according to Micheli.
 “It’s certainly common to have competing ballot measures. It’s a little less common to have measures with a so-called ‘poison pill’ in it,” Micheli said. 
 The three competing ballot measures appear side by side on ballots this year, although voters may not realize that Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 will nullify the billionaire tax.
 Lester Black/SFGATE Public polling has fluctuated throughout the campaign on the three measures, but all three propositions have cleared a 50% majority in various polls. If those polls are simultaneously accurate, they imply, based on simple arithmetic, that at least some voters are supporting both the billionaire tax and the poison pill propositions that could block it.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Micheli said voter confusion on the matter is likely. 
 “If they’re just glancing at a quick summary or looking at the title and summary, it may not be so clear,” Micheli said.
 That’s led supporters of the billionaire tax to amplify their message in the campaign’s final weeks. Tim Connors, an influencer in New York City, warned his followers in an Instagram video that Propositions 41 and 42 were a “final Hail Mary” from the billionaires that could actually work.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 “The kicker is that polls are showing a similar level of support for all three. They are trying to confuse you, and we’re not going to let them,” Connors said. His video has since been shared 20,000 times.
